questions.question: Distinguish direct from alternating current with South African figures, explain where AC comes from, and explain why high voltage reduces losses in transmission.
questions.expected_answer: Direct current from a cell or solar panel flows steadily one way at a constant voltage such as 1.5 or 12 volts; alternating current from a generator and the mains swings smoothly between positive and negative, in South Africa fifty times a second at 50 hertz, with the socket voltage swinging between about plus and minus 325 volts, equivalent in heating to a steady 230 volts. AC arises naturally in a rotating generator because the magnetic field through each coil grows, shrinks and reverses once per revolution, so 3000 revolutions a minute gives 50 cycles a second. The grid uses AC because its voltage can be changed easily by transformers. Wires have resistance and waste power as heat in proportion to the square of the current, and since power is voltage times current the same power can be sent as a small current at high voltage with far smaller losses; sending a city's power at 230 volts would need millions of amps and impossibly thick cables, while 400 000 volts cuts the current by nearly two thousand times and the losses by that factor squared, though it must be stepped back down before reaching houses because it would be lethal.

questions.question: Explain how a transformer works, how the turns ratio determines step-up or step-down with examples along the grid, and why a transformer gives no free power and works only on AC.
questions.expected_answer: A transformer is two coils on a shared iron core with no electrical connection between them; AC in the primary coil creates a magnetic field in the core that grows, collapses and reverses fifty times a second, and this changing field induces an alternating voltage in the secondary coil whose size is set by the ratio of turns, so twice the turns gives twice the voltage and a tenth the turns a tenth. A step-up transformer has more secondary turns and raises a generator's roughly 20 000 volts to 275 000 or 400 000 volts for transmission; step-down transformers have fewer secondary turns and lower the voltage at substations to 132 000 or 88 000, then 11 000 for streets, then 230 volts at the pavement kiosk or pole-mounted can, with a phone charger's transformer taking it to five volts. Energy is conserved, so when voltage rises by a factor the current falls by the same factor and volts times amps is nearly equal on both sides, less a few percent lost as heat and hum, which is why large transformers are oil-filled with cooling fins. Steady DC produces a steady field that induces nothing, so transformers work only on AC, which is why the grid is AC; the symbol is two facing coils with lines between them for the core.

questions.question: Trace the path of electricity from power station to socket with the voltages at each stage, describe the national grid and who operates it, and explain the role of frequency and load shedding.
questions.expected_answer: Generators at a power station or a wind farm's collector substation produce AC at some thousands of volts; a step-up transformer in the switchyard raises it to transmission voltage, mostly 275 and 400 kilovolts with a few 765 kilovolt lines, the highest in Africa; transmission lines on steel pylons carry three phase conductors plus an earthed shield wire, held clear by long insulators, forming the national grid operated by the National Transmission Company, formerly part of Eskom, which links every station to every region so a trip in one province is covered within seconds from another and imported hydro reaches the cities. Transmission substations step down to 132 or 88 kilovolts for sub-transmission, distribution substations run by Eskom or municipalities step down to 11 or 22 kilovolts along streets, and a final pole or kiosk transformer gives 230 volts single-phase to houses or 400 volts three-phase to factories, from where a cable feeds the meter and distribution board with main switch, earth-leakage unit and breakers. Generation must equal consumption at every instant and frequency is the signal: excess demand slows generators and drops frequency below 50 hertz, and if it falls too far protective relays disconnect and the system can collapse into a blackout lasting days, so load shedding deliberately disconnects some areas in rotation to keep the rest at 50 hertz, watched second by second from the control room.
